blocks.title: You'll want to know: 愿意

segments.text: 愿意 — yuànyì — "to be willing (to)".
要是你愿意我们明天就去 yàoshi nǐ yuànyì wǒmen míngtiān jiù qù — If you're willing, we'll go tomorrow.

The new character, in pieces: 愿 (yuàn) — fourteen strokes in four pieces: a bar and a long stroke falling to the left, like a cliff; under it 白, five strokes, and 小, three strokes; and 心 at the foot, four strokes. The next lesson puts it in your hand.

愿意 (yuànyì) is built from 愿 (yuàn) and 意 'what one means', both inherited from Middle Chinese, ngjwonH and 'iH (Guangyun, in Baxter's transcription), which glosses the first 'to desire' and 'to think of'.
One more word for saying what would happen.

blocks.title: Script — a cliff over 白 and 小, then 心

segments.text: 愿 (yuàn).
Four pieces: the cliff, then what it shelters, then 心 at the foot. Count the pieces, not the strokes.
The cliff, two strokes: a bar, then a long stroke falling to the left down from its left end.

Under the cliff, 白, five strokes, then 小, three strokes, as you wrote them: a short stroke falling to the left, a vertical, a bar that turns down, two short bars; then a vertical that hooks to the left, a short stroke on its left and a dot on its right.
心, four strokes, as you wrote it, across the foot: a dot, a long curve that hooks up, then two dots.
2 + 5 + 3 + 4 = fourteen.

segments.text: 愿望 — yuànwàng — "a wish one has; a desire".
如果可以有一个愿望你想要什么 rúguǒ kěyǐ yǒu yí ge yuànwàng nǐ xiǎng yào shénme — If you could have one wish, what would you want?
愿望 (yuànwàng) is built from 愿 (yuàn) 'to desire' and 望 'a hope', both inherited from Middle Chinese, ngjwonH and mjangH (Guangyun, in Baxter's transcription).
One more word for saying what would happen.

zhǐyào nǐ nǔlì jiù néng rúyuàn — As long as you work hard, you'll get what you hoped for.
如愿 (rúyuàn) is built from 如 'as, like' and 愿 (yuàn) 'a wish', both inherited from Middle Chinese, nyo and ngjwonH (Guangyun, in Baxter's transcription): as one wished.
One more word for saying what would happen.

我们自愿在这儿工作 wǒmen zìyuàn zài zhèr gōngzuò — We work here of our own free will.
自愿 (zìyuàn) is built from 自 'self' and 愿 (yuàn) 'to wish', both inherited from Middle Chinese, dzijH and ngjwonH (Guangyun, in Baxter's transcription), which glosses the first 'from' and 'by way of'.

blocks.title: You'll want to know: 但愿

segments.text: 但愿 — dànyuàn — "let us hope that; if only".
但愿他明天能来 dànyuàn tā míngtiān néng lái — Let's hope he can come tomorrow.

但愿 (dànyuàn) is built from 但 'only' and 愿 (yuàn) 'to wish', both inherited from Middle Chinese, danX and ngjwonH (Guangyun, in Baxter's transcription), which glosses the first as a grammar word and 'merely': I only wish.
One more word for saying what would happen.
